text: Kepler, excited to have Jack Woodruff with me. Quickly introduce yourself. Yeah, hi, I'm Jack Woodruff. I am the founder and former CIO of Candlestick Capital Management, a long-short equity hedge fund based in Greenwich, Connecticut. Before founding Candlestick, I was a partner and portfolio manager at Surveyor Capital, which is a division of Citadel. Very cool. Thanks, Jack. So the reason we did this this way is we've had this conversation before, and I think this is one of the most enlightening folks to chat with, given that Jack has spent his career picking stocks in an environment that's changing more than it ever was before. So we'll treat this really as a fireside chat. So, Jack, paint the picture for us. What does fundamental investing look like in the age of AI, say five years from now? Well, it's hard to say. Like, long-term stock picking, I don't believe is really going to change much at all. There's always been a mosaic, and there's always been alpha creation by finding a divergent view. So that isn't going to change at all. I think that that still will stay the same. Now, how people synthesize all of the information and where table stakes go to in terms of, like, what everybody has, and then how you synthesize that data is going to change completely. The roles, the traditional roles of, say, a portfolio manager or an analyst are going to be completely thrown upon their heads. And I still think it's, like, too early to say what that's all going to look like, as these tools are just so new, especially to the users. You've got a lot of people doing a few things, but it's just not clear to me. That it's like we're there and, oh my gosh, it's going to be these new things. Like, we have a bunch of other things to kind of talk about, but I think it's going to be super fascinating to watch how it all plays out. Very cool. So at Citadel, you had 18 people covering 400 stocks, and at Candlestick, you had 30 stock pickers. Could one great analyst cover all 400 by 2030? So the biggest issue is humans are still the bottleneck. I mean, like, at the end of the day, you have to get the information into your head. So it's really all about sort of how man and machine can work together. Investment management is a time management exercise. What I mean by that, if I spent all of my time working on one stock, that'd be great. I'd probably know it better than anyone else in the world. But, like, if there wasn't anything to do in that stock, I'd be kind of—there isn't much to do. Well, if I do two, well, then I have half as much time and so forth until I go. So you start getting diminishing returns on how much time you could spend on any particular stock. So, you know, what can AI do? Can AI help me cover more names? Perhaps. Maybe it allows me to raise the table stakes on what I just kind of, like, have as a general knowledge, because that work used to take me hours to prepare to get me ready for what it was, and now maybe, you know, an AI program can, you know, help me prepare a lot of that work in five minutes, which used to take me six to eight hours. So that allows me to do other things. Again, like it's a very competitive industry, so it's not like if I get rid of all these people or if I have like five analysts, whereas before I had 30, yeah, maybe those people can do more. But now all of a sudden this opens up other time. This opens up time that I could spend doing either more proprietary research, channel checks, more sort of like...
